clinicalPearls: A recurrence of pericarditis after a symptom-free interval following a first episode, typically presenting with the same pleuritic chest pain that eases on sitting forward
Most cases are presumed immune-mediated following an initial viral or idiopathic episode, and an autoinflammatory mechanism is increasingly recognised
Diagnosis rests on recurrent pericarditic pain with supportive features such as a friction rub, typical electrocardiographic changes, a new or worsening effusion, or a rise in inflammatory markers
Colchicine added to anti-inflammatory therapy reduces the risk of further recurrences and is a cornerstone of treatment
Corticosteroids relieve symptoms but promote steroid dependence and further relapses, so they are reserved for specific indications and used sparingly
Refractory, corticosteroid-dependent disease may respond to interleukin-1 blockade, reflecting the autoinflammatory basis
The long-term outlook is generally good, and progression to constriction is uncommon in idiopathic recurrent disease
reference.pathophysiology: Recurrent pericarditis usually follows an initial acute episode of viral or idiopathic pericarditis and is thought to reflect a dysregulated immune or autoinflammatory response rather than persistent infection. Inflammation of the pericardial layers produces the characteristic pleuritic pain, a friction rub, and often a small effusion, with release of inflammatory mediators, particularly the interleukin-1 pathway, driving relapses. Incomplete treatment of the first attack and early or high reliance on corticosteroids favour recurrence. Repeated inflammation can occasionally lead to pericardial thickening, but in idiopathic disease progression to significant constriction is unusual.
additionalDifferentials: Pericarditis from systemic autoimmune disease such as lupus
additionalInvestigations: Electrocardiography for widespread saddle-shaped ST elevation and PR depression
Inflammatory markers including C-reactive protein to confirm activity and guide tapering
Echocardiography to detect and size a pericardial effusion and assess for tamponade
Cardiac MRI to demonstrate pericardial inflammation and late gadolinium enhancement in uncertain cases
Targeted screening for autoimmune or systemic causes when features suggest secondary disease
redFlags: Signs of cardiac tamponade such as hypotension, raised jugular venous pressure, and pulsus paradoxus
A large or rapidly accumulating pericardial effusion
Features of evolving constriction with right heart failure
Troponin rise or ventricular dysfunction indicating significant myocardial involvement
reference.prognosis: Most patients have a favourable long-term outcome with control of recurrences, and although relapses can be troublesome and prolonged, progression to constrictive pericarditis is rare in idiopathic recurrent disease.
pitfalls: Early or excessive use of corticosteroids, which fosters dependence and further recurrences
Omitting colchicine, thereby losing its proven protection against relapse
Stopping anti-inflammatory therapy abruptly rather than tapering guided by symptoms and C-reactive protein
Advising undue restriction of activity or missing an underlying systemic autoimmune cause
references: Braunwald's Heart Disease: A Textbook of Cardiovascular Medicine
ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of pericardial diseases
management: First-line anti-inflammatory therapy with an NSAID or aspirin plus gastric protection, tapered as symptoms and C-reactive protein settle
Add colchicine as a cornerstone for a prolonged course to reduce further recurrences

Reserve corticosteroids at the lowest effective dose with slow taper for specific indications such as NSAID contraindication, connective-tissue disease or pregnancy, given their tendency to promote steroid dependence and relapse
Use interleukin-1 blockade with anakinra or rilonacept for corticosteroid-dependent, colchicine-resistant disease reflecting its autoinflammatory basis
Restrict exercise until symptoms resolve and inflammatory markers normalise

Monitor with serial C-reactive protein and echocardiography to guide tapering and detect effusion or tamponade, screening for and treating underlying systemic causes and referring refractory cases to a specialist pericardial service
